title: Sfincione
subtitle: Sicilian thick-crust pizza with onion, anchovy, and breadcrumbs
excerpt: Sfincione is the Sicilian version of pizza: a thick, spongy dough topped with onion, tomato, anchovies, and a crunchy layer of toasted breadcrumbs. It is baked in a tin, not on a stone, and the result is soft inside and crisp on top and bottom.
sourceNotes: Sfincione is the street food of Palermo, sold warm from the backs of vans across the city. The name derives from the Latin 'spongia', meaning sponge, which describes the thick, open-crumbed dough. The traditional version uses caciocavallo cheese, which is difficult to find outside Sicily; pecorino or aged provolone is the standard substitution.

recipe.yieldDescription: 1 large sfincione, about 30 x 40 cm, serving 6 to 8
recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in slices wrapped individually. Reheat from frozen in a 200°C oven for 12 to 15 minutes.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The dough needs 3 hours to prove at room temperature. Start in the morning to bake in the afternoon.
recipe.temperatureNote: Fan or conventional. Preheat the oven with the oiled tin inside.

content.text: Sfincione is Sicilian pizza: thick dough, a slow-cooked onion and tomato sauce, anchovy fillets pressed into the topping, and a layer of seasoned breadcrumbs that turns golden and crunchy in the oven. It is baked in an oiled tin rather than on a stone, and the dough ends up thick and spongy inside with crisp edges. Sfincione is more substantial than Neapolitan pizza and usually eaten in slices as a snack rather than a full portion.
Mix the flour, yeast, and salt. Add the water and 2 tablespoons of olive oil. Knead for 8 minutes until smooth. Oil the bowl, cover, and leave at room temperature for 2 to 3 hours until doubled.

While the dough proves, cook the onions: fry in 2 tablespoons of olive oil over low heat for 25 minutes, stirring often, until soft and golden. Add the tinned tomatoes, crush them roughly, and cook for a further 15 minutes until thick. Season with salt and dried oregano. Cool.
Oil a large rectangular baking tin (about 30 x 40 cm) generously. Tip the dough in and press it out to fill the tin with your oiled fingers. Leave to rest for 20 minutes.

Spread the onion and tomato sauce evenly over the dough. Press the anchovy fillets into the sauce at even intervals. Scatter the grated pecorino over the top, then scatter the breadcrumbs. Drizzle with a little more olive oil.
Bake at 220°C for 30 to 35 minutes until the breadcrumbs are deep golden and the base is crisp when you lift a corner with a palette knife. Cool in the tin for 10 minutes before cutting into squares.

Sfincione is the street food of Palermo, sold warm from carts and vans across the city. The Palermitano version uses caciocavallo, a semi-firm pulled-curd cheese from Sicily. Outside Sicily, pecorino or aged provolone gives a similar salty, slightly sharp character. The word sfincione comes from the Latin for sponge and describes the thick, open-textured dough that absorbs the onion-tomato sauce without becoming soggy.
